steps.ask: One angle is a right angle and the other two are written in terms of A. What must the three angles add to?
steps.title: Use the angles of a triangle

lines.text: The angles of a triangle add to $\hl{1}{180^\circ}$. The right angle is $\hl{3}{90^\circ}$, so the other two angles add to $\hl{3}{90^\circ}$.

problems.note: Now there are several triangles, and each angle you find is used in the next triangle. The 180° rule is the same as before, applied again and again.

legend.2: the unknown angle (A, B or C)

steps.ask: Which angle is vertically opposite to A at the crossing? What do vertically opposite angles have in common?
steps.title: Find A

lines.text: $A$ and the $\hl{3}{60^\circ}$ angle are vertically opposite angles, so they are equal.

steps.ask: The top triangle has two known angles now. What do its angles add to, and what does that leave for B?
steps.title: Find B

lines.text: $B$, $A$ and $\hl{3}{75^\circ}$ are the angles of the top triangle. The angles of a triangle add to $\hl{1}{180^\circ}$.

steps.ask: Which angle at k matches the 60° angle at j? What is the angle inside the bottom triangle that is on a straight line with it?
steps.title: Find the angle inside the bottom triangle at line k

lines.text: The $\hl{3}{60^\circ}$ angle at $j$ corresponds to the $\hl{3}{60^\circ}$ angle at $k$. The angle inside the bottom triangle is on a straight line with it.

steps.ask: The bottom triangle has a 120° angle, a 40° angle and C. What do its three angles add to, so what is C?
steps.title: Find C

lines.text: The angles of the bottom triangle add to $\hl{1}{180^\circ}$.

legend.2: the unknown angle α or β

steps.ask: α is opposite the angle SPQ. What do opposite angles of a parallelogram have in common?
steps.title: Find α

lines.text: Opposite angles of a parallelogram are equal, so $\hl{2}{\alpha}$ equals $\hl{1}{|\angle SPQ|}$.

steps.ask: β and the angle SPQ share a side. What do adjacent angles of a parallelogram add to?
steps.title: Find β

lines.text: Adjacent angles of a parallelogram add to $\hl{3}{180^\circ}$.

problems.note: The angles are now expressions in x and y, so each rule gives an equation and you solve them one after the other. The two rules are the same as in problem 1.

steps.ask: (2x − 30)° is opposite the 100° angle. What do opposite angles of a parallelogram tell you?
steps.title: Opposite angles are equal: find x

lines.text: $(2\hl{2}{x}-30)^\circ$ is opposite the $\hl{1}{100^\circ}$ angle, so they are equal.

steps.ask: (x + 3y)° and 100° are next to each other on one side. What do adjacent angles add to, and what does that give you for x + 3y?
steps.title: Adjacent angles sum to 180°

lines.text: $(\hl{2}{x}+3\hl{2}{y})^\circ$ and $\hl{1}{100^\circ}$ are adjacent angles, so they add to $\hl{3}{180^\circ}$.

steps.ask: x is known now. Which equation still has y in it, and how do you get y from it?
steps.title: Substitute x = 65 and solve for y

legend.2: the unknown corner T (its x and y values)

steps.ask: Which side is equal and parallel to [FB]? How far, and in which direction, is T from Q?
steps.title: Use the opposite sides of the parallelogram

lines.text: In $FBQT$, the side $[TQ]$ is parallel and equal to $\hl{1}{[FB]}$. $\hl{1}{[FB]}$ goes straight up 5 units, so $\hl{2}{T}$ is 5 units directly below $Q$.

steps.ask: Where does T sit now? Plot it and check the four corners form a parallelogram.
steps.title: Plot T

lines.text: Plot $\hl{2}{T(-2, 2)}$ and join $F$, $B$, $Q$ and $T$ to see the parallelogram.

steps.ask: PQRS is a square. Which other pair of corners moves in the same way as S to P? Then how far do x and y change?
steps.title: Find the translation that takes S to P

lines.text: $PQRS$ is a square, so $S \to P$ is the same move as $R \to Q$.

legend.2: the unknown: the image L, the length |LM| and the line

steps.ask: L is the reflection of M in the y-axis. What happens to the coordinates of M?
steps.title: Find L using the symmetry about the y-axis

lines.text: $\hl{2}{L}$ is the reflection of $\hl{3}{M(9, 1)}$ in the $\hl{1}{y}$-axis, so $\hl{2}{L = (-9, 1)}$.

steps.ask: What do you notice about the y-values of L and M, and how does that give the length |LM|?
steps.title: (i) Find the length of LM

lines.text: $\hl{2}{L}$ and $\hl{3}{M}$ have the same $y$-value, so the length is the difference in $x$-values.

steps.ask: What do all the points on LM have in common, and what is the equation of a line like that?
steps.title: (ii) Write the equation of LM

lines.text: Every point on $LM$ has $\hl{2}{y = 1}$, so the horizontal line is $\hl{2}{y = 1}$.
